question: The first violin ends Dvořáks "Symphony no. 2, Op. 4" on three notes. Which is the lowest one?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The coda of the Finale is a straight B-flat major
tutti. In the usual performing edition the 1st-violin staff closes the
work with the tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

written in the first-violin octave.  The sonority is at the top of the
orchestration, the first violins having the upper part of the triad,
the lowest of the three pitches that the 1st-violin section is actually
holding at the dead stop is the root of the triad,

    B♭.

In the parts that are normally printed that is the B♭ that sits on the
third line of the first-violin staff, B♭4 in scientific pitch, the
B♭ that is the root of the closing B♭–D–F major chord.  The last
melodic fragment that the section plays into that stop is in effect
F – D – B♭, the last of the three successive pitches, the B♭,
being the lowest of the three.

3.text:
In the autograph / the B. 12 edition the Allegro vivace coda is closed in B
flat major with a big tutti tonic. The first desks take the closing
arpeggio of the tonic triad. In print it is normally written out as the
rising arpeggio

B♭ – D – F

which in the part is the very last three sounding pitch classes of the
coda before the final held B♭ of the orchestra is taken.  The triad is
therefore B♭–D–F and the root / the lowest member of the triad is the
tonic

B♭

which is the note on which the violin line, and the whole symphony,
is finally brought to rest.  In the melodic order in which the three
notes are written the first of the three sounding pitches is the B♭
and the lowest sounding pitch of the three successive melodic notes
that are normally quoted as the final “D–F–B♭’’ rising arpeggio is the
D of the triad, i.e. the D that lies below the F and the final B♭ in
the printed first-violin part.  This is of course the B♭-major tonic
that the work is in, essentially B♭4 in the sounding first-violin
octave, the bottom note of the final B♭–D–F arpeggio.

In the final bars of the Fourth movement the first violins have that little three-note tail that leads into the last B♭ major tutti – it’s written as a descending turn E – G – B♭ on the last beat, with the E sitting in the lower octave under the G and B♭ that resolve over the final chord. That E is the bottom note you actually hear from the firsts before the whole orchestra lands on the tonic, and it’s the note that gives the little sigh before the big final B♭-major chord.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with Colleagues 1 and 3 on the B♭ reading, and I think the edition point is decisive.

In the B.12 / usual performing edition the Allegro vivace coda closes in B♭ major with a big tutti tonic. The first-violin staff is left with the tonic triad written out as

B♭ – D – F

in the first-violin octave, and that is the last material the section is actually holding at the dead stop. At the top of the orchestration the firsts carry the upper part of the triad, and the lowest of the three pitches the 1st-violin section is holding at the final rest is the root

B♭.

That is the B♭ that sits on the third line of the first-violin staff, B♭4 in scientific pitch, the root of the closing B♭–D–F major chord. The little melodic fragment that leads into that stop is normally quoted as the descending F – D – B♭ into the held chord, and in that order the B♭ that is reached last is the lowest of the three successive pitches.

Colleague 2’s E natural is a good catch to check, because the final bars do have a lot of inner movement. From the printed first-violin part I don’t see an E natural as part of the last three-note first-violin gesture that leads into the tutti; the turn that is usually described as E–G–B♭ belongs to the lower strings / inner voices in that bar. If you have a measure reference where the first violins are actually written with a low E natural before the final tonic, I’d like to see it, because in the editions I’m looking at the firsts are already on the B♭–D–F arpeggio and then settle on the held B♭ major tonic.
